businessModel: B2B payments SaaS: software subscription plus payment-volume take-rate; serves mid-market finance teams for accounts-payable automation and embedded payouts. Hybrid SaaS + transaction revenue.
sourceNote: Synthetic stress-test case engineered to stress the engine's ability to distinguish a GO_TO_MARKET_MISALIGNMENT (expansion/land-and-expand motion failing) from a generic retention or pricing story. The owner intake frames the issue as 'competitors and pricing pressure'; the evidence shows the expansion engine (upsell/cross-sell) has stalled while gross retention is fine. Tests whether the engine isolates the expansion motion, not the product or price. Not historical; metrics representative.

ownerIntake.businessType: B2B payments SaaS for mid-market finance teams (AP automation + embedded payouts). Founded 2019, total raised $26M. Revenue model: per-seat software subscription plus a take-rate on processed payment volume. Current ARR $8.0M, 50% YoY growth, 310 customers.
ownerIntake.stage: ARR $8.0M, 50% YoY growth. Gross retention healthy at 94%. Net revenue retention fell from 110% to 100% over four quarters. Gross margin 68% (blended software + payments). New-logo win rate stable. Expansion bookings as a share of total bookings dropped from 38% to 19%. Cash runway 26 months at $480k/month burn.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Reaccelerate net revenue retention back above 110% and protect take-rate margins against larger entrants; reach Series B metrics ($15M ARR, NRR >110%) within 15 months.
ownerConstraints: Funding constraint: $26M raised, 26-month runway at $480k/month burn; the next raise is gated on NRR re-expansion, so expansion economics are the headline metric.

Product constraint: cross-sell modules (embedded payouts, virtual cards, FX) exist and are technically live, but only ~30% of AP-automation customers have ever been pitched them; integration effort to activate a module averages 3 weeks of customer-side work.

Organizational constraint: 54 staff (14 engineering, 12 sales all on new-logo quota, 8 CS, 6 support, rest G&A). There is no account-management or expansion-sales function; CS is success-only and not quota-carrying.
Market constraint: two larger payments platforms have entered mid-market with aggressive take-rate discounts on high-volume tiers; they target the same finance-team buyer.
Commercial constraint: ~65% of revenue is software subscription and ~35% is payment take-rate; the take-rate line is where competitors compete on price.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: NRR has slid 110%→100% over a year and expansion bookings collapsed from 38% to 19% of bookings, even though gross retention is healthy at 94% and new-logo acquisition is fine. The owner believes larger competitors are undercutting take-rates and pressuring pricing and wants to cut take-rates to defend volume. But the data shows the company simply is not running an expansion motion: most customers have never been offered the cross-sell modules, and there is no expansion-quota owner. The owner must decide in 30 days whether to cut take-rates company-wide or rebuild the expansion engine before the next board update on NRR.

businessProblem: A B2B payments SaaS growing 50% has a deteriorating expansion engine: NRR fell from 110% to 100% and expansion bookings collapsed from 38% to 19% of bookings, while gross retention (94%), new-logo win rate (~31%), and product satisfaction (NPS 44) all held steady. The owner reads this as price pressure from larger discounting entrants and wants to cut take-rates across the board. But the cross-sell modules that should drive expansion are barely sold: payouts attached to 22% of the base, virtual cards 9%, FX 6%, with only ~30% of AP customers ever pitched a second module, and the company has zero expansion-quota or account-management capacity. Competitive take-rate losses are confined to the top 10% highest-volume prospects, not the broad base. With NRR gating the Series B raise and 26 months of runway, the owner must choose within 30 days between a margin-eroding blanket price cut and rebuilding a structured expansion motion.

evidence.finding: Net revenue retention fell from 110% to 100% over four quarters while gross retention stayed healthy at 94%. The entire NRR decline is therefore attributable to lost expansion, not to customers leaving. Expansion bookings dropped from 38% to 19% of total bookings over the same period.
evidence.source: NRR cohort report, bookings ledger split by new vs expansion

evidence.finding: There is no expansion motion. All 12 sales reps carry new-logo quota only; CS (8 people) is success-only with no expansion target; there are zero account-management or expansion-quota holders. Only ~30% of AP-automation customers have ever been pitched a second module. Cross-sell penetration is low: embedded payouts 22%, virtual cards 9%, FX 6%, despite QBR-recorded customer interest.
evidence.source: Sales compensation plans, CRM pipeline analysis, QBR notes

evidence.finding: Two larger payments platforms entered mid-market with aggressive take-rate discounts. However, the competitive losses on price are concentrated in the top 10% highest-volume prospects, where take-rate dominates economics; the broad mid-market base shows no elevated price-driven loss. New-logo win rate is stable at ~31%.

Cross-sell modules (payouts, virtual cards, FX) are technically live and product satisfaction is high (NPS 44, stable). Customers express interest in additional modules in QBRs, but there is no follow-through pipeline because no one owns expansion. The constraint is commercial motion, not product readiness or customer willingness.
evidence.source: Product analytics, NPS survey, QBR notes

evidence.finding: Revenue mix is ~65% subscription and ~35% payment take-rate at 68% blended margin. A blanket take-rate cut to match entrants would hit the 35% take-rate line across the entire base to defend against losses concentrated in the top 10% of prospects, an asymmetric trade that would compress margin far more than it protects revenue.
